people.seed: Baptist pastor's wife, 52, Texas, homeschools, politically conservative
people.desc: Donna Kessler lives outside Waco and has been married for 26 years to the pastor of a Southern Baptist church of about 180. She homeschooled all four of her children with a young-earth science curriculum, and the youngest is now 15. She teaches the women's Bible study, keeps chickens, laughs loudly and has a quick tongue she often regrets. Her mother died of cancer two years ago, and she sobbed through the funeral in front of the whole congregation without apology.

notes.note: Her morning quiet time is precious to her, but so is the fellowship of the church. She would say both, so Not sure is the nearest.
Corrie ten Boom hiding Jews comes to mind at once, and so does Rahab. But she has spent twenty years teaching her children that lying is always a sin. She would want to say it depends.
Slightly loaded for her. 'Really belongs to them' sounds like the government taking her things. She believes in giving generously, just not that the extra is owed.
Confusing: does 'books' mean the Bible? If it does, she disagrees strongly. If it means ordinary books, she might agree. She guessed it meant the Bible.
She wants the government to protect Christians and honor God. She does not want a state church; her husband preaches religious liberty. 'Support' could mean either.
Saved by grace alone, so she disagrees. But growing in holiness takes real work, so she stopped short of strongly.

people.overall: It felt friendly and quick, and she liked that it was not trying to trick her. A few statements made her want to add a sentence, especially the ones on lying and nature.

kindred.name: Gregory the Great
kindred.hook: Chosen pope in a plague year, he was getting ready to slip away into hiding when he was seized and carried to St Peter's to be consecrated, and he spent the next thirteen years writing letters about how the job had wrecked his peace while he fed Rome, bargained with invading armies and sent monks to convert the English.
lines: "Anger at real wrongdoing can be a good thing." You: Strongly agree. Gregory the Great: "For if there was no anger originating in virtue, Phinees would never have allayed the fierceness of God's visitation by his sword. Because Eli lacked such anger, he quickened against himself the stirrings of the vengeance of the Most High to an implacable force." (Morals on the Book of Job)

"A Christian can fight in a just war with a clear conscience." You: Strongly agree. Gregory the Great: "And report goes that it is not from a desire of shedding blood that you constantly court these wars, but for the sake of extending the republic in which we see that God is worshipped, to the end that the name of Christ may be …" (Register of Letters, to Gennadius, exarch of Africa)

"In the end, God will save everyone." You: Strongly disagree. Gregory the Great: "Certain it is, and without all doubt most true, that as the good shall have no end of their joys, so the wicked never any release of their torments" (Dialogues)

sparring.name: Origen
sparring.hook: As a teenager he was so set on dying with his arrested father that his mother hid all his clothes to keep him home.
lines: "Many Bible stories matter more for their deeper meaning than for what literally happened." You: Strongly disagree. Origen: "I do not suppose that anyone doubts that these things figuratively indicate certain mysteries, the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally." (On First Principles)

"A Christian can fight in a just war with a clear conscience." You: Strongly agree. Origen: "And none fight better for the king than we do. We do not indeed fight under him, although he require it; but we fight on his behalf, forming a special army--an army of piety--by offering our prayers to God." (Against Celsus)

"In the end, God will save everyone." You: Strongly disagree. Origen: "But our belief is, that the Word shall prevail over the entire rational creation, and change every soul into His own perfection; in which state every one, by the mere exercise of his power, will choose what he desires, and obtain what he chooses." (Against Celsus)

people.seed: Catholic night-shift nurse, 34, Manila, devout, tired
people.desc: Maricel Dizon works nights in the ICU of a public hospital in Quezon City and sends a third of her pay home to her parents in Iloilo. She is the eldest daughter, unmarried, and saving for the exam that would let her work in the UK. She prays the rosary on the jeepney, keeps a Santo Nino on her locker shelf, and has a dark ward humour that keeps her going. As a teenager she wanted to enter the convent, but her father fell sick and the family needed her wage.

notes.note: She believes it is right in principle, but she would never confront someone directly; it would shame them. Not sure covers the gap between belief and practice.
Confusing: she read it as staying calm at work, which she needs every night. She was not sure it meant the heart in general. Her agree is about work.
A Filipino proverb came to mind: God gives the mercy, people do the work. So she agreed, but she would add 'with God's help'.
She has never thought about it and was too tired to work it out. Not sure is honest but empty.
This one hurt. She felt called to the convent and stayed to support her family. She does not know if she was right, and no answer says that. Not sure is a sore spot, not an opinion.
She hopes so for her patients, but the priest says hell is real. Not sure.

people.overall: Easy to answer on a break, and most of it was about everyday life, which she liked. The statement about following a calling against your family stopped her for a long moment.

kindred.name: Antony the Great
kindred.dates: c. 251 to 356 (the Life says he died about 105 years old)
kindred.hook: At eighteen he heard one Gospel verse read in church, walked out, gave away three hundred acres of farmland, and spent the next eighty-odd years in the desert, where emperors wrote to him and he hardly bothered to reply.
lines: "A good hearty laugh is good for the soul." You: Strongly agree. Antony the Great: "The old man said to him: So it is also in the work of God. If we stretch the brothers beyond measure, they quickly break. So one must, now and then, come down to meet the brothers." (Sayings of the Desert Fathers , alphabetical collection)

"The ideal is a heart so calm that strong feelings never stir it." You: Agree. Antony the Great: "for it was neither contracted as if by grief, nor relaxed by pleasure, nor possessed by laughter or dejection, for he was not troubled when he beheld the crowd, nor overjoyed at being saluted by so many." (Life of Antony)

"God still speaks to people through dreams." You: Strongly agree. Antony the Great: "The vision of the holy ones is not fraught with distraction: For they will not strive, nor cry, nor shall any one hear their voice. But it comes so quietly and gently that immediately joy, gladness and courage arise in the soul." (Life of Antony , Antony's sermon to the monks)

sparring.name: Jerome
sparring.dates: born c. 347 at Stridon (on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia); died 30 September 419 or 420 at Bethlehem
sparring.hook: Feverish in the desert, he dreamed he stood before Christ's judgment seat and heard "You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ", was flogged, and woke, he swore, with bruised shoulders: the man who then gave the West its Latin Bible also wrote some of the angriest letters in Christian history.
lines: "Even if you believe you'll see them again, it's right to weep openly for someone you've lost." You: Strongly agree. Jerome: "Yours are detestable tears, sacrilegious tears, unbelieving tears; for they know no limits, and bring you to the verge of death." (Letter 39, to Paula, on the death of Blaesilla)

"A good hearty laugh is good for the soul." You: Strongly agree. Jerome: "Leave to worldlings the privileges of laughing and being laughed at. One who is in your position ought to be serious." (Letter 130, to Demetrias)

"The ideal is a heart so calm that strong feelings never stir it." You: Agree. Jerome: "a state in which the mind ceases to be agitated and — to speak simply — becomes either a stone or a God." (Letter 133, to Ctesiphon)

people.seed: Orthodox convert, 28, Ohio, software engineer who reads the Church Fathers online
people.desc: Nathan Brooks is a backend engineer at an insurance company in Columbus. He grew up in a nondenominational church, drifted into agnosticism at college, and was chrismated at an Antiochian parish three years ago; his parents are still hurt by it. He reads the Fathers on New Advent late at night, keeps the fasting calendar in a spreadsheet he rarely manages to follow, and knows he can be a know-it-all at coffee hour. Privately he finds the case for universal salvation compelling and has never said so at church.

notes.note: He remembered a Chrysostom homily saying Christ is never recorded laughing, and wondered if the statement was a test. He agreed anyway, because he likes laughing.
The desert writers say anger's proper use is against demons and your own sins. 'Real wrongdoing' could mean other people's, so he could not commit.
He is drawn to the desert and to stillness, but he also believes no one is saved alone and the Liturgy is the heart of it. Agree is a lean, not a view.
He knows the Fathers disagree: Chrysostom defends a helpful deception, Augustine forbids every lie. Not sure is honestly where he is.
Loaded for him in a strange way. It sounds like the Fathers' ideal of freedom from the passions, but it describes it wrongly, as feeling nothing. No answer says 'that is the wrong definition'.
God can, and the saints' lives are full of it. But he has been taught to distrust his own dreams. Not sure is the nearest.
The wording feels Protestant. His church bars people from communion rather than putting them out, so neither answer fits cleanly.
He thinks it can be allowed, but St Basil advised soldiers who killed to stay away from communion for a time. It is the 'clear conscience' he disagrees with.
He believes God and the person work together. 'Mostly up to you' goes too far, so he disagreed, but 'not up to you' would be wrong too.
He may hope it, he cannot say it. Not sure is exactly right, though he knows it is a dodge.

people.overall: He enjoyed it and kept trying to spot which Father sat behind each statement. He wanted a comment box on about a third of them, and the one on calm hearts annoyed him.

kindred.name: Isaac the Syrian
kindred.hook: Made bishop of Nineveh, he quit after five months and spent the rest of his life in the mountains, writing that a merciful heart burns with love for every creature, animals, enemies and even demons, until it cannot bear to hear of anything suffering.
lines: "Most of the time, it's better to say less." You: Strongly agree. Isaac the Syrian: "Love silence above all things. It brings thee near the fruit which the tongue is too weak to interpret. At first we compel ourselves to be silent. Then from our silence something is born which draws us towards silence." (Mystic Treatises)

"If you believe God is calling you, follow, even if your family begs you not to." You: Strongly agree. Isaac the Syrian: "The blessed one, however, was not to be persuaded even at this time, when natural mercy usually is stirred, to transgress the voluntary borders, saying: ,If I go out, my heart will not be pure before God, for I despise visiting spiritual brethren, should I …" (Mystic Treatises)

"You grow closer to God alone and in quiet than among other people." You: Agree. Isaac the Syrian: "Compare not all powers and signs that are worked in the whole world, with a man’s consciously sitting in solitude." (Mystic Treatises , Six Treatises on the Behaviour of Excellence)

sparring.name: Basil the Great
sparring.dates: c. 330 to 379 (died 1 January 379 by the traditional reckoning; some scholars prefer 377 or 378)
sparring.hook: When the emperor's prefect threatened him with confiscation, exile, torture and death, Basil answered that a man who owns only rags and a few books cannot be robbed, that all the earth is God's, and that death would only send him to God sooner.
lines: "Some questions about God are better left alone." You: Strongly agree. Basil the Great: "It follows then that to investigate syllables is not to shoot wide of the mark, nor, because the questions raised are what might seem to some insignificant, are they on that account to be held unworthy of heed." (On the Holy Spirit)

"A good hearty laugh is good for the soul." You: Agree. Basil the Great: "Since the Lord condemns those that laugh it is obvious that there is never a time of laughter for the believer, especially when there is so great a multitude of those who by transgression of the law dishonour God and are dead in sins, for …" (The Shorter Rules)

"You grow closer to God alone and in quiet than among other people." You: Agree. Basil the Great: "Whose feet then wilt thou wash ? Whom wilt thou care for? In comparison with whom wilt thou be last if thou livest by thyself?" (The Longer Rules)

people.seed: Worship leader at a charismatic non-denominational church, 24, Nashville
people.desc: Kayla Ruiz grew up Assemblies of God in Tampa and moved to Nashville to study music at Belmont. She now leads worship at a church of about 1,500 and pays the rent as a barista and a session singer. She keeps a journal of prophetic words people have given her, sees a Christian therapist, and cares about racial justice and caring for creation. Her father walked away from the faith when she was sixteen, and she still prays for him every day.

notes.note: She loves the 'secret place' with God, and she also lives for the Sunday room when the whole church is worshipping. It is both for her.
Yes if you have the relationship and speak the truth in love; no if it means calling people out. The statement does not say which.
Sunsets and mountains preach to her. But 'as much as from books' made her pause, because the Bible is the Word. She agreed, not strongly.
She believes God welcomes our questions, so she disagreed. Yet some things are holy mystery. A mild disagree is near enough.
She believes the stories happened and also that they mean something. 'More than' made her rank them, and she would not.
She has never thought about it. Not sure is genuine.
She thought of her dad. She wants it to be true but does not see it in the Bible. Not sure.

people.overall: Fun and fast. The ones on dreams, tears and the body felt like her, and the ones on war and governments felt like someone else's quiz.

kindred.name: Augustine of Hippo
kindred.hook: As a boy of sixteen he stole a load of pears he did not even want and threw them to the pigs, and thirty years later he spent pages of his life story trying to work out why.
lines: "Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith." You: Strongly agree. Augustine of Hippo: "Moreover, if those who are called philosophers, and especially the Platonists, have said anything that is true and in harmony with our faith, we are not only not to shrink from it, but to claim it for our own use from those who have unlawful …" (On Christian Doctrine)

"There's nothing wrong with being rich, as long as you use it well." You: Strongly agree. Augustine of Hippo: "In this Scripture it is covetousness that is condemned, not gold, or silver, or riches, but covetousness." (Sermon 61)

"The ideal is a heart so calm that strong feelings never stir it." You: Strongly disagree. Augustine of Hippo: "And if that is to be called apathy, where the mind is the subject of no emotion, then who would not consider this insensibility to be worse than all vices?" (The City of God)

sparring.name: John Cassian
sparring.hook: After years among the holiest monks of Egypt, he admitted that alone in his cell he still lost his temper, at his pen for being too thick, at his knife for being blunt, and at his flint when it would not spark.
lines: "The ideal is a heart so calm that strong feelings never stir it." You: Strongly disagree. John Cassian: "For the end and aim of patience consists, not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all." (Institutes)

"Most of the time, it's better to say less." You: Disagree. John Cassian: "For this is the first practical step towards learning, to receive the regulations and opinions of all the Elders with an earnest heart, and with lips that are dumb; and diligently to lay them up in your heart, and endeavour rather to perform than to …" (Conferences)

"Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith." You: Strongly agree. John Cassian: "a special hindrance to salvation is added by that knowledge of literature which I seem already to have in some slight measure attained, in which the efforts of my tutor, or my attention to continual reading have so weakened me that now my mind is …" (Conferences)

people.seed: Reformed seminary student, 26, Grand Rapids, loves a good argument
people.desc: Pete Vander Molen grew up in the Christian Reformed Church, decided it had gone soft, and is now in his second year of an M.Div. at a confessional seminary in Grand Rapids. He works part-time in a used theology bookshop, smokes a pipe on his porch, and argues infant baptism online until his wife takes his phone away; their first baby is due in March. He loves Bavinck and Kuyper, so he is happy to learn from unbelieving scholars, and he is a firm cessationist. He laughs easily and never takes a disagreement personally.

notes.note: He agrees with James that people should be slow to speak, and he laughed at himself because he never is. Not sure is half a joke.

He holds a firm view that none of the answers express: every lie is a sin, but you are not bound to tell a murderer everything, and Rahab was praised for her faith, not her lie. He wanted 'yes, but' and chose Not sure.
Loaded for him: 'really belongs to them' seems to deny that property is real. He believes you must give generously, but not that the extra is theirs. So a mild disagree.
He thought of the Belgic Confession: creation is a book about God, but Scripture shows Him more clearly. 'As much as' is what he disagrees with.
Scripture says the secret things belong to the Lord, so he agrees. But he suspects the phrase is often an excuse to stop thinking.
Confusing to him: a real call is tested and confirmed by the church, not just believed privately. 'If you believe' is the sticking point.
He is genuinely torn between the original Westminster Confession and the American revision of it, and would happily argue either side. Not sure is honest.

people.overall: He enjoyed it and wanted to argue with half of it, which he counts as a compliment. The lying statement frustrated him because it had no room for the distinction he cares about.

kindred.dates: c. 330 to 379 (died 1 January 379 by the traditional reckoning; some scholars prefer 377 or 378)
kindred.hook: When the emperor's prefect threatened him with confiscation, exile, torture and death, Basil answered that a man who owns only rags and a few books cannot be robbed, that all the earth is God's, and that death would only send him to God sooner.
lines: "Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith." You: Strongly agree. Basil the Great: "So we, if wise, shall take from heathen books whatever befits us and is allied to the truth, and shall pass over the rest." (Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature)

"Many Bible stories matter more for their deeper meaning than for what literally happened." You: Strongly disagree. Basil the Great: "I know the laws of allegory, though less by myself than from the works of others. There are those truly, who do not admit the common sense of the Scriptures, for whom water is not water, but some other nature" (Hexaemeron)

"A church should put out members who won't live by its standards." You: Strongly agree. Basil the Great: "In Corinth the man that had his father’s wife, though accused of nothing else except this only, is not only himself handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh until he should correct his sin by worthy fruits of repentance, but involves the …" (On the Judgment of God , his preface to the Morals)

sparring.hook: As a teenager he was so set on dying with his arrested father that his mother hid all his clothes to keep him home.
lines: "God still speaks to people through dreams." You: Strongly disagree. Origen: "many have been converted to Christianity as if against their will, some sort of spirit having suddenly transformed their minds from a hatred of the doctrine to a readiness to die in its defense, and having appeared to them either in a waking vision or …" (Against Celsus)

"Many Bible stories matter more for their deeper meaning than for what literally happened." You: Strongly disagree. Origen: "I do not suppose that anyone doubts that these things figuratively indicate certain mysteries, the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally." (On First Principles)

"A Christian can fight in a just war with a clear conscience." You: Strongly agree. Origen: "And none fight better for the king than we do. We do not indeed fight under him, although he require it; but we fight on his behalf, forming a special army--an army of piety--by offering our prayers to God." (Against Celsus)

people.seed: Retired Methodist schoolteacher, 71, Ohio, progressive, gardener
people.desc: Peg Hollis taught fourth grade for 34 years in a small town outside Columbus and was widowed three years ago. When her lifelong United Methodist congregation left the denomination in the split, she drove twenty minutes to one that stayed, and she still grieves the friends it cost her. She keeps a huge vegetable garden and a pollinator bed and leaves bags of tomatoes on her neighbours' porches all August. She is warm, talkative and stubborn, her late father fought in Korea, and she has made peace with not knowing why her husband got sick.

notes.note: Depends entirely on who and what. With a child in her class, yes; with a grown friend she would rather pray and wait to be asked. 'Not sure' is really 'it depends'.
She believes in sharing and gives her extra away, but 'really belongs to them' is stronger than she would put it. Agree was the nearest.
She thought of her granddaughter joining a strict group that told her to cut off her family. 'Calling' can mean something beautiful or something dangerous, so she hovered.
Grace comes first, but you have to cooperate with it. Neither side fits; she leaned disagree because 'mostly up to you' leaves God out.
She hopes so with all her heart but will not claim to know. Agree stands for hope, not certainty.

people.overall: Quick and pleasant, like the questions people argue over at a church potluck. A few times she wanted a 'Yes, but' button.

kindred.name: Gregory of Nyssa
kindred.hook: He forged letters from his uncle to patch up a family feud, got caught more than once, and his brother Basil wrote to tell him he was too simple to be trusted; he became the boldest mind of his family, the one who hoped even the devil would be healed.
lines: "Your body is a friend to look after, not an enemy to fight." You: Strongly agree. Gregory of Nyssa: "The inefficiency of the body from either cause will be that which it guards against; it will train the flesh, neither making it wild and ungovernable by excessive pampering, nor sickly and unstrung and nerveless for the required work by immoderate mortification." (On Virginity)

"Many Bible stories matter more for their deeper meaning than for what literally happened." You: Strongly agree. Gregory of Nyssa: "the Divine intention lies hid under the body of the Scripture, as it were under a veil, some legislative enactment or some historical narrative being cast over the truths that are contemplated by the mind." (Against Eunomius)

"Even if you believe you'll see them again, it's right to weep openly for someone you've lost." You: Strongly agree. Gregory of Nyssa: "In no other way can the burning heart cool down, swelling as it is with its affliction, unless it relieves itself by sobs and tears." (Funeral Oration on Meletius)

sparring.name: Tertullian
sparring.dates: born c. 155-160; writing 196/197 to after 220; Jerome says he lived to a decrepit old age
sparring.hook: He wrote a whole book urging Christians to be patient, and opened it by confessing that he himself was "ever sick with the heats of impatience".
lines: "Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith." You: Strongly agree. Tertullian: "What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? What between heretics and Christians? Our instruction comes from the porch of Solomon, who had himself taught that the Lord should be sought in simplicity of heart." (The Prescription against Heretics)

"Even if you believe you'll see them again, it's right to weep openly for someone you've lost." You: Strongly agree. Tertullian: "For why should you grieve, if you believe that (your loved one) is not perished? Why should you bear impatiently the temporary withdrawal of him who you believe will return? That which you think to be death is departure." (On Patience)

"Many Bible stories matter more for their deeper meaning than for what literally happened." You: Strongly agree. Tertullian: "And, indeed, if all are figures, where will be that of which they are the figures? How can you hold up a mirror for your face, if the face nowhere exists?" (On the Resurrection of the Flesh)

people.seed: Agnostic philosophy graduate, 30, London, curious about Christianity but unconvinced
people.desc: Hannah Petrakis has an MA in philosophy from King's College and works as a copy editor at an academic press in Bloomsbury. Her mother is Greek Cypriot Orthodox and her father lapsed Church of England; she stopped going to anything at fifteen. She reads Augustine and Simone Weil on the Tube, goes to evensong at St Paul's for the music, and keeps a notebook of lines she cannot argue her way out of. She dislikes vague statements, votes left, and keeps the God question open mostly because it will not stay closed.

notes.note: She has no experience of growing closer to God either way. 'Not sure' here means 'I don't accept the premise', not hesitation, and the quiz cannot tell the difference.
You learn a great deal about the world from nature; whether that is learning about God is exactly the open question. 'Not sure' is the premise problem again.
'Still' assumes God once did. She disagreed with the assumption as much as with the claim, and was not sure which she was answering.

She thinks some wars are just, but reading the Sermon on the Mount as an outsider she thinks a consistent Christian could not fight. She answered what she thinks Christianity implies, not her own view of war. Unclear which the quiz wanted.
She cannot say what a God she does not believe in will do. If there is one worth the name, she would hope yes. 'Not sure' is the only option and it hides that hope.
'Your job' is too strong. It depends on the wrong and how close you are.
Moral luck: upbringing, temperament and circumstance do a lot of the work. 'Mostly' decides it and she could not tell how much weight it carries.

people.overall: More interesting than she expected, and not preachy; the statements are clear and short. But about five of them assume God exists, and each time she had to decide whether to answer hypothetically, as a Christian would, or as herself, and the quiz never said which.

kindred.name: Origen
kindred.hook: As a teenager he was so set on dying with his arrested father that his mother hid all his clothes to keep him home.
lines: "Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith." You: Strongly agree. Origen: "The children of the philosophers speak of geometry and music and grammar and rhetoric and astronomy as being ancillary to philosophy; and in the same way we might speak of philosophy itself as being ancillary to Christianity." (Letter to Gregory)

"Many Bible stories matter more for their deeper meaning than for what literally happened." You: Strongly agree. Origen: "I do not suppose that anyone doubts that these things figuratively indicate certain mysteries, the history having taken place in appearance, and not literally." (On First Principles)

"Lying can be the right thing to do if it protects someone." You: Strongly agree. Origen: "But a man on whom necessity imposes the responsibility of lying is bound to use very great care, and to use falsehood as he would a stimulant or a medicine, and strictly to preserve its measure, and not go beyond the bounds observed by Judith …" (Stromateis , book 6 , quoted by Jerome in Apology against Rufinus)

sparring.name: Gregory the Great
sparring.hook: Chosen pope in a plague year, he was getting ready to slip away into hiding when he was seized and carried to St Peter's to be consecrated, and he spent the next thirteen years writing letters about how the job had wrecked his peace while he fed Rome, bargained with invading armies and sent monks to convert the English.
lines: "Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith." You: Strongly agree. Gregory the Great: "This thing we took so much amiss, and so strongly disapproved it, that we changed what had been said before into groaning and sadness, since the praises of Christ cannot find room in one mouth with the praises of Jupiter." (Letters)

"Lying can be the right thing to do if it protects someone." You: Strongly agree. Gregory the Great: "This kind of lying also those that are perfect eschew with the greatest care, so that not even the life of any man should by deceit of theirs be defended, lest they hurt their own souls, whilst they busy themselves to give life to another’s …" (Morals on the Book of Job)

"Governments should use their power to support the Christian faith." You: Strongly disagree. Gregory the Great: "Make haste to extend the Christian faith among the peoples under your sway, redouble the zeal of your rectitude in their conversion, put down the worship of idols, overturn the edifices of their temples" (Letter to King Æthelberht of Kent)

people.seed: Pentecostal mother of four, 41, Lagos, runs a small shop
people.desc: Funmilayo Adebayo runs a provisions and phone-credit shop in Ikorodu and is a house-fellowship leader in a Redeemed Christian Church of God parish. Her husband works at a logistics firm near Apapa port, and she wakes at five to pray in tongues before opening the shutters. She tithes on every naira but has no patience for pastors who buy jets, and she learned her bookkeeping from the Lebanese wholesaler she buys from. She tells everyone about the dream that warned her off a bus to Ibadan in 2014, the week that bus crashed.

notes.note: Confusing. She read it as the perfect peace God gives and agreed at once. Only afterwards did she wonder whether it meant never weeping or rejoicing in worship, which she would strongly reject.
Lying is sin, full stop, but she thought of Rahab and of what she would say to armed robbers at her gate asking where her children sleep. Disagree, not strongly.
The extra belongs to God first. She gives, and gives a lot, but not because it is theirs. The statement's reason is wrong even where the practice is right.
The body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, so look after it; but the flesh is an enemy you crucify. The statement mixes body and flesh, so she agreed with half of it.
Jesus wept, so yes; but her church teaches not to mourn like those without hope, and long open weeping is gently discouraged. Agree, not strongly.

In Nigeria 'government supporting a religion' also means states funding Islam in the North. She wants the government to protect Christians and be fair, not to push one faith. No answer quite fits; loaded toward a Western reading.
Loaded for her: 'more than what literally happened' sounds like saying the stories did not happen. She believes they happened AND carry deep meaning, and the 'more than' made her pick a side.

people.overall: Easy, she answered most in a second, and it felt like the questions they discuss at house fellowship. The lying and government ones made her think of real life in Lagos, and she is not sure she read the calm one right.

His family demanded to know how God could have a Son, and he had to find answers. He dislikes leaving questions alone, though he admits some of what is said about the Trinity can't be fully explained.
His head says a church should hold a standard. But he knows what it is to be put out of a community, and that decided it: Disagree.
He believes a person must come to Christ. His mother came to mind at once, and he tapped Disagree with difficulty.

kindred.hook: Feverish in the desert, he dreamed he stood before Christ's judgment seat and heard "You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ", was flogged, and woke, he swore, with bruised shoulders: the man who then gave the West its Latin Bible also wrote some of the angriest letters in Christian history.

(Letter 70, to Magnus, an orator of Rome)

(Evagrius Ponticus, Praktikos, chapter 92, as quoted by Socrates Scholasticus, Church History)

(Life of Antony)

He agreed, but because questions about God aren't worth his time, not out of reverence.

He answered as if the church were any organisation with values: you let go of people who won't live by the culture.
He isn't a Christian, so he answered for the Christians he knows.

kindred.name: John Cassian
kindred.hook: After years among the holiest monks of Egypt, he admitted that alone in his cell he still lost his temper, at his pen for being too thick, at his knife for being blunt, and at his flint when it would not spark.

John Cassian: "For this is the first practical step towards learning, to receive the regulations and opinions of all the Elders with an earnest heart, and with lips that are dumb; and diligently to lay them up in your heart, and endeavour rather to perform than to …" (Conferences)

John Cassian: "For if we seek our own, and want obstinately to keep what is good for ourselves, we must even in urgent cases of this sort speak the truth, and so become guilty of the death of another: but if we prefer what is for another's …" (Conferences)

"Becoming a good person is mostly up to you." You: Strongly agree. Augustine of Hippo: "And my whole hope is only in Your exceeding great mercy. Give what You command, and command what You will." (Confessions)

"Most of the time, it's better to say less." You: Strongly agree. Augustine of Hippo: "I began to be more grieved at having refrained from saying what I ought to have said, than I had before been grieved by having said what I ought not." (Expositions on the Psalms, Psalm 39)

people.seed: Mennonite nurse, 48, Lancaster County

Basil the Great: "It follows then that to investigate syllables is not to shoot wide of the mark, nor, because the questions raised are what might seem to some insignificant, are they on that account to be held unworthy of heed." It hit a nerve. She agreed with what she is working toward in recovery, not with how she feels about her body most days.

Only for serious, unrepentant sin after due process, and by Scripture's standards rather than 'its standards'.
